headline: A Big Bookstore Arrives Near a Shop on the Corner. This Isn’t a Movie.

paragraphs.text: Walking between the new mother-daughter-owned bookstore, the Rabbit Books and Bar, at East 11th Street and Avenue A and the new, big Barnes & Noble catty-corner, Julia DeMarco observed life imitating art.

“It reminds me of a movie,” said Ms. DeMarco, 29, who lives in the East Village. “Meg Ryan runs an independent bookstore, and Tom Hanks opens this big conglomerate nearby and puts her out of business.”

With apologies for that spoiler, the movie Ms. DeMarco referred to is the 1998 romantic comedy “You’ve Got Mail,” directed by Nora Ephron. On Monday night inside the Rabbit, its co-owner Marianna Vaidman Stone squeezed her eyes shut and pressed her hands into a tabletop at the utterance of its name.

“Of course I saw the movie,” she said. And she estimated that “You’ve Got Mail” was now mentioned more in online comments about her store than, for example, its poetry gatherings, wine list or comfortable reading nooks.
“I intend,” Ms. Vaidman Stone added, “for my ending to be different.”
The Rabbit opened on Aug. 11. The Barnes & Noble followed on Nov. 18. Some bibliophiles cheered.
“They’re both a welcome addition for their own unique reasons,” said Karen Martinez, an East Village resident for 20 years.

Coming on the heels of an article in The Atlantic that declared “The End of Reading Is Here,” bookstore openings come across as New York City’s vigorous rebuttal. Businesses and events that sell and glorify books are surging. Recently in these pages, readers (yes, readers) have learned about a 66-hour live recitation of Robert Caro’s “The Power Broker,” a new “Moby Dick”-themed bar and neighborhood book crawls.
Now the staredown between the Rabbit and the Barnes & Noble — which is the city’s biggest new bookstore in a decade — has some pondering how sustainable in-person book buying is.
“Is there a market for this many bookstores?” Chris Brown, a 28-year-old Stuyvesant Town resident, asked as he exited the Rabbit. “I wonder who will survive the longest.”
In response to emailed questions, a Barnes & Noble spokesperson said that the stores would complement more than they would compete, and that their proximity was a boon for both.
“Bookstores attract book buyers,” the spokesperson wrote.

Blaming Barnes & Noble for burying independent bookstores may actually seem quaint now, with the explosion of Amazon and online book sales. In 2018, the New York Times columnist David Leonhardt was moved to write, “It’s plausible that Barnes & Noble will not survive.” Once ubiquitous around New York City, by 2023 Barnes & Noble had only three stores left in Manhattan and one in Brooklyn.

After Amazon recast Barnes & Noble as David instead of Goliath, book lovers began cheering the chain as proof that physical bookstores would not vanish. A 2022 Times headline noted that Barnes & Noble had gone “from villain to hero.” Nationwide, the chain has expanded from fewer than 600 stores in 2023 to more than 740 today, per a news release from a Barnes & Noble media contact, Debb Hanks (no relation to Tom).

Its resurgence, though, is not universally welcomed. On Avenue A, people could be heard shouting at the gleaming displays in the windows, “Shop local!” John Dorney, 28, said the new store felt “predatory.”

Still, other neighbors who pride themselves on supporting independent businesses conceded that if a chain store had to move into that long-vacant 11,000-square-foot space, this was far from the worst.
“If we’re going to have a new, big shop, I’m glad it’s a bookstore,” said Anna Levak, 56, after she strolled through the new Barnes & Noble with her 14-year-old daughter, Lila.

Amenities that used to give Barnes & Noble an advantage over smaller competitors are inverted on Avenue A. It is the Rabbit that has the cozy bar, plush sofas, and tables for cappuccinos, cabernets, snacks and book-themed board games. While the Barnes & Noble does have colorful, cushioned sitting cubes in its large children’s section, the store otherwise has only a few hardwood chairs — and no food, drink or restrooms.
“They’re going to put the Barnes & Noble out of business,” Amar Jivraj, 28, gloated upon leaving the Rabbit.

Ms. Vaidman Stone, 55, said she hoped the stores could serve as “the gateway to the literary playground of the East Village.” Born in Moscow, Ms. Vaidman Stone fled antisemitism in the Soviet Union to emigrate to the United States with her family in 1979. Her grandfather and father later opened an American gas station and incorporated it under the letters “KROL” — the root of the word “krolik,” which in Russian means “rabbit.” The small, clever animal became a family totem.

When Ms. Vaidman Stone decided to switch careers from public policy work to creating “a book-centered place of human connection,” she named it to honor her family. The name is also a homage to the world’s diverse array of literature, so much of which features rabbit characters — from ancient folklore to “Alice in Wonderland” and “Watership Down.”

In January, she signed her 10-year lease for an ample corner space, previously filled by a 7-Eleven, across Avenue A from a vibrant new country music bar, Lucinda’s. When she learned that Barnes & Noble would open catty-corner, she called it “a blow.”
Her daughter and co-owner, Emily Stone, looked on the bright side.
“I’m happy to have more bookish people in the area,” said Ms. Stone, 25, as she poured a customer a glass of rosé.
